concept.name: Averaging up
concept.definition: Buying additional shares of an existing position at successively higher prices, raising the average cost basis while increasing exposure to a rising asset. It is the mirror of averaging down and the discrete-time cousin of pyramiding into strength.
concept.intuition: Leaning into winners trades a worse average price for a bigger position in a confirmed trend - you pay up precisely because the market is validating the thesis.
concept.mechanics: Add tranches at predetermined higher price points or on technical triggers such as moving-average breaks or momentum readings. Each add raises the cost basis, so the position becomes increasingly sensitive to a reversal from the peak.
concept.formula: Average cost = sum(q_i x p_i) / sum(q_i); equal buys at $20, $24, $28, and $32 give a $26 basis.
concept.failure_modes: Buying into late-stage momentum risks adding just before exhaustion; a sharp reversal puts the later, higher-priced tranches underwater immediately, and rising concentration compounds the loss.
concept.misconceptions: That averaging up is always reckless; disciplined versions predetermine add points and total size, whereas the undisciplined version is simply chasing. It is also distinct from dollar-cost averaging, which is price-agnostic rather than momentum-following.
concept.example: Buying XYZ at $20 and then equal amounts at $24, $28, and $32 yields a $26 basis; a drop to $25 loses money on the whole position even though the first tranche is still up 25%.
